item.title: Why Is Mexico Defying Latin America’s Right Turn?
item.description: How Mexico’s left has managed to retain strong support is a key question of contemporary Latin American politics. The most likely answer centers on the ruling Morena party’s pragmatic brand of left-wing politics, which combines bold redistributive policies, greater security, and a willingness to compromise in the name of both.

item.title: The Digital-Currency Divide
item.description: The rush to develop central bank digital currencies has slowed as underwhelming demand and mounting costs have given governments second thoughts. But while the Federal Reserve and other central banks have shelved their plans, the European Central Bank is pressing ahead with its digital euro.

item.title: The ASEAN Paradox
item.description: As the Association of Southeast Asian Nations gathers for its 49th Summit, several rifts have exposed the group’s institutional shortcomings. But amid a fracturing global order, ASEAN must choose: turn its convening authority into concerted action or be reduced to an arena for great-power rivalry.

item.title: Medical AI Needs Bedside Manners
item.description: Even the most accurate medical AI tools have little value if they make patients uneasy or doctors find them too cumbersome. A comfort-by-design approach could overcome these obstacles by involving patients and practitioners in development and ensuring that new systems work with existing medical practices.

item.title: Reviving the Legacy of Reykjavík
item.description: As nuclear threats grow, AI accelerates, and international law comes under strain, the world urgently needs a renewed commitment to dialogue. Today's leaders can find a template in the landmark 1986 summit between then US President Ronald Reagan and Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev.

item.title: Europe’s AI Dreams Exceed Its Grid
item.description: Europe is racing to expand its AI data-center capacity, but its power grids are already strained, and local communities are increasingly pushing back against new construction. Achieving technological sovereignty will require less grandstanding and more practical solutions that make better use of existing resources.

item.title: What the US Midterms Could Mean for AI
item.description: Now that the Democrats will hold sizable majorities in both chambers of the US Congress, they have an opening to push for long-overdue legislation to steer AI development toward the common good. Private companies should not have the power to decide unilaterally which risks the public will bear.

item.title: Let’s Publish AI-Generated Articles!
item.description: Peer-reviewed academic journals exist to advance our knowledge and understanding by publishing the best work being done in a given field. If that is the goal, and the best reviewers—both human and AI—agree that an article generated by AI meets that standard, why should a journal's editors reject it?

item.title: The AI Industry Should Make Something People Want
item.description: AI companies have alienated Americans by forcing them to bear the costs of their products while treating their consent as optional. With voters across the United States rejecting data centers, the incoming Congress has an opportunity to enact meaningful regulation and hold the industry accountable.

item.title: It’s the Corruption, Stupid
item.description: Fed up with Donald Trump and his family's blatant profiteering, Americans dealt Republicans a resounding defeat in this month’s midterm elections. Democrats won by linking corruption to the cost-of-living crisis, but the party’s establishment remains compromised and must clean house before 2028.

item.title: AI Investors Have Overlooked Obvious Risks
item.description: Prior to the US midterm elections on November 3, financial markets had been treating generative AI as some kind of unstoppable force that could not be hampered by higher interest rates or political and social resistance. But now reality may be setting in.

item.title: The Mismeasure of Privacy
item.description: Over the past few decades, we have adopted a new framework for thinking about privacy that centers our experience in the digital realm, conflates privacy with secrecy, and fails to account for the insecurity surveillance generates. As a result, even privacy advocates often undermine their own cause.

item.title: The Right Lessons From Brazil and the US
item.description: One lesson progressives in both countries cannot afford to ignore is that recent election results do not amount to a mandate. Neither the Democrats in the US nor President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s Workers' Party in Brazil are offering a vision voters can get excited about.

item.title: A Russian Bribe the Size of Europe
item.description: US President Donald Trump is willing to sacrifice Ukraine in exchange for lucrative oil and gas deals with Russia, but this bargain is bound to backfire spectacularly. Vladimir Putin has a long record of betraying his business partners, and once he gets what he wants from Trump, Europe will be his next target.

item.title: Will Anthropic’s IPO Lead to Better AI Regulation?
item.description: When frontier AI labs go public, ordinary people’s investments and pensions become tied to their valuations and stock prices. While excessive regulation could undermine a firm’s growth, catastrophic accidents caused by inadequate safety measures could do the same—and wipe out shareholder value.

item.title: A Minimum Basic Income Is Not Enough
item.description: The rise of AI is concentrating wealth and political power in fewer and fewer hands, making extreme inequality a threat to democracy itself. A universal basic share that gives ordinary people a portion of global profits could help narrow the growing gap between billionaires and everyone else.

item.title: Scott Bessent’s Risky Short-Termism
item.description: The US Treasury secretary's commitment to accelerate buybacks of longer-term debt and issue more short-term debt in their place promises significant budgetary savings. But if borrowing costs rise, what happens in the T-bill market won’t stay in the T-bill market.

item.title: Why Trump Crowned the Man Who Cost Him Congress
item.description: By appointing Stephen Miller to be his chief of staff, US President Donald Trump has revealed what he cannot give up after decisive midterm losses. The moral depravity of one of the most widely reviled members of his administration is the citadel he will defend until the end.

item.title: Why Politicians Love Stimulus Checks
item.description: Stimulus checks sent to households promise to supercharge the economy, but much of the money simply sits in people's bank accounts. They are popular with voters but do little to address the underlying causes of economic downturns and leave future generations to foot the bill.

item.title: Who’s Winning (and Who’s Losing) the Ocean? — Marie-May Jeremie
item.description: Ahead of COP31, PS sat down with Marie-May Jeremie, Minister of Environment, Climate, Energy and Natural Resources of the Republic of Seychelles, to discuss the logic of “blue” economic development. Watch as she describes the deeply personal stakes for small island states, and calls on the global community to support their efforts.
